events.title: The cornerstone of new St. Peter's
events.shortBlurb: Pope Julius II laid the first stone of the basilica that would rise over the tomb of the Apostle…
body: On 18 April 1506 Pope Julius II descended into the foundations beside the old Vatican basilica and laid the first stone of the new St. Peter's. The ancient church, built by the Emperor Constantine over the tomb of the Apostle in the fourth century, had stood for some twelve hundred years and was leaning and in danger of collapse.

The first design, by Donato Bramante, imagined a great central church crowned by a dome; the work would pass through the hands of Raphael and Antonio da Sangallo before Michelangelo, appointed chief architect in 1546, gave the building its definitive form, including the mighty dome completed after his death in 1590.

The vast cost was met in part by the preaching of indulgences, whose abuses in Germany helped provoke Luther's protest of 1517. The finished basilica was consecrated by Urban VIII on 18 November 1626, one hundred and twenty years after the first stone, and remains the centre of Catholic worship and pilgrimage.

events.title: Luther before the Diet of Worms
events.shortBlurb: Summoned to recant, Martin Luther refused to disown his writings before the emperor and the empire…
body: On 18 April 1521 Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar already excommunicated by Rome, stood for the second time before the Diet of Worms and the twenty-one-year-old Emperor Charles V. Summoned under a safe conduct won by his prince, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, he had acknowledged the day before that the twenty-five books laid on the table were his, and had asked a day to consider his answer.

Asked again whether he would recant, he refused. Unless convinced by the testimony of Scripture or by clear reason, he declared, his conscience was captive to the Word of God, and he could not and would not recant, 'since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience'. The famous 'Here I stand, I can do no other' is traditional but probably a later addition.

On 25 May the emperor issued the Edict of Worms, branding Luther a notorious heretic and banning his writings. By then Frederick's men had spirited him away in a feigned ambush to the Wartburg, where, hidden under the name of Junker George, he spent ten months translating the New Testament into German.
